extracted.intended_audience: War Department/Quartermaster/Comptroller officials, government attorneys, and accountants managing Army appropriations
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical rules for when and how various Army appropriations (transportation, contingencies, construction, support of the Army, Military Academy, fortifications, etc.) may be charged for specific expenses; includes tests, examples, and exceptions from Comptroller/Attorney General decisions. Intended to guide charging decisions and departmental budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use for authorized purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation must be expended only for the objects and purposes for which it was made; expenditures not within the scope of the appropriation are improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples throughout text illustrate that the intended statutory purpose controls availability; e.g., an appropriation for 'construction' does not permit purchase of an already-constructed building unless language authorizes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific appropriation precludes use of other appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress has made a specific appropriation for a purpose, the use of any other appropriation for that same purpose is thereby precluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by decisions holding an appropriation 'for expenses of recruiting' cannot be used to pay mileage due a recruiting officer which is payable from 'Pay, etc., of the Army.' Also contingencies cannot be used to make up deficiencies in specific appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction appropriation does not buy already-constructed buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation specifically provided 'for the construction of buildings' will not be available for the purchase of buildings already constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decision: appropriation for construction, operation, and maintenance of laundries would not cover purchase of a post-exchange laundry building with machinery and fixtures (C.15026, Jan. 22, 1912).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditures on lands without title allowed if benefit assured
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no legal objection to expenditure of public money on works of improvement on lands to which title has not been acquired in the absence of a statute forbidding it, provided the Government will be assured that the benefit of the expenditure will be received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: appropriations for Army transportation or 'Roads, walks, wharves, and drainage' expended on public highways, sidewalks; monument could be erected without acquiring title to site; easement may suffice for levee or pipeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easement suffices where full title not acquired
rubrics_metrics.description: An easement in private land is sufficient to permit construction (e.g., levee, pipeline) without acquisition of full title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions held it was unnecessary to obtain title before constructing a levee; an easement was sufficient (C.5089, Oct. 7 & Nov. 4, 1898; C.14719, Jan. 31, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military-purpose utility justifies charging civil-looking repairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Where repair of a public highway or similar work is useful for military purposes, the expense may be a legal charge against appropriate Army appropriations despite ordinary highway maintenance being a civil obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that repair of a public highway running through a military reservation, if useful for military purposes, may be charged to Army transportation appropriations (C.3683, Nov. 27, 1897; C.20373, Apr. 28, 1910).

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel expenses incident to execution/supervision charged to project appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specific appropriation is made for a work of improvement, travel expenses incurred in the supervision or execution of such work are presumed intended to be borne by that appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inspection travel for increasing West Point water supply charged to the construction appropriation; travel for manufacture/inspection of torpedoes charged to 'Purchase of submarine mines and necessary appliances' (C.16459; C.13728).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Authorized by law" in incidental expenses requires statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'authorized by law' in an appropriation for incidental expenses refers to statutory authority; expenditures without such authority cannot be paid from that appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rental of ground for light artillery practice not authorized by law could not be paid from 'Incidental expenses of the Quartermaster's Department' but could be charged to contingencies (62 P., 208, Nov. 2, 1893).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingencies appropriation three-part test
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant expenditures from 'Contingencies of the Army' the object of expenditure: (1) must be necessary, useful, or appropriate to the Army proper; (2) must have the character of an incidental, casual, unforeseen, or emergency expense; and (3) must not come within the scope of any other appropriation for the support of the military establishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test governs permissive uses of the contingencies fund; many illustrative permitted and forbidden examples are provided (C.7030; C.27145).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingencies fund cannot supplement a specific appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriation for contingencies is not available to supplement a specific appropriation for furnishing certain supplies or rendering certain services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: where repairs appropriation for the old Ford Theater was insufficient, contingencies could not be used to supply the deficiency (62 P. 74, Oct. 19, 1893).

rubrics_metrics.name: Army and Military Academy appropriations are distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriations for the support of the Army and those for the support of the Military Academy are distinct and separate; funds appropriated for one cannot be used to defray the expenses of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: West Point is both a military post and a military academy; Army appropriations may be expended for strictly Army purposes at West Point. Examples of allowed Army charges at West Point and disallowed items (architect services, supplementing Academy pay) are given (C.11106; C.10689; C.18009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Army support funds at installations that are also schools
rubrics_metrics.description: When an installation (e.g., War College at Washington Barracks) is a military post and intended for instruction, general appropriations for support of the Army may cover necessary work even if the specific construction appropriation is exhausted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: grading, removing rubbish, underground electrical connections charged to general Army appropriations when War College located at a military post (C.20719).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of transportation charging test for fortifications vs transportation appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a means of transportation is planned as an integral and inseparable part of a fortification project (and appropriate to be under exclusive control of combatant force), its construction and maintenance is chargeable to fortification appropriations; otherwise the cost should be borne by Army transportation appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule stated with citation (C.13998, Feb. 17, 1903).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation appropriation covers transport of materials and personnel for military business
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriation for 'Transportation of the Army' may bear expenses such as transportation of baggage of officers on military duty, movement of units to expositions when treated as military, transport of cadets, transport of insane prisoners to government hospitals, dredging to enable landing of troops and supplies, salvage claims on government property transported in private vessels, carriage hire incident to official calls, and similar military-necessity transports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples listed (C.10587; C.10825; C.10863; C.20052; C.21602; C.17725; C.26396; C.25821). But the line is sometimes discretionary and depends on whether the Secretary regards the trip as public business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation appropriation does not cover certain returns after civil arrest
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses of returning a soldier who was arrested by civil authorities and later discharged by them are not a charge against the appropriation for Army transportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision holding returning such a soldier to his proper station not chargeable (C.2529, Mar. 20, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of transporting materials to a construction site charged to construction appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where material for a specific construction project is purchased separately, the cost of transporting that material to the project site should be paid from the appropriation for the construction of the building, not from the general transportation appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: material purchased on Puget Sound for Alaskan quarters — transport cost charged to construction appropriation; if contractor agreed to transport material free, still charged to construction appropriation (C.18314; C.25056).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mining and transporting government coal charged to transportation appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of mining coal at a Government coal mine, carrying it to tidewater, and transporting it to place of use should be charged against the appropriation for 'Transportation of the Army.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C.21659, Oct. 12 & Nov. 10, 1908.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidental expenses appropriation limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Items within an 'Incidental expenses' appropriation must be 'authorized by law' (statutory authority). If not statutorily authorized, the expense cannot be paid from that appropriation but may be charged to contingencies when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by rental for light artillery practice (not authorized by law) which could not be paid from incidental expenses but could be charged to contingencies (62 P., 208).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingencies: many permissible small or extraordinary charges
rubrics_metrics.description: The contingencies appropriation has been used for a variety of necessary or emergency expenses appropriate to the Army proper — e.g., carriage hire in presidential funeral, engraving cannon, awarding national trophies, appliances for field sports during World's Fair, witness fees/mileage for Army investigations, supplies during forest fires, salaries/expenses of Secret Service member detailed to assist military, expenses of civilian lecturers whose notes remain as textbooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long list of permitted examples (C.11438; C.10443; C.14668; C.14991; C.28241; C.27395; C.18866; C.14278). The three-part test must still be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingencies fund not available for non-military civilian expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The contingencies appropriation is limited to Army proper needs and is not available for expenses of purely civilian character (e.g., medical treatment or burial of civilian employees engaged in non-military work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of denied charges: medical treatment of a civil employee injured on non-military work; burial expenses of civilian employees; transporting Canadian half-breed Indians (44 P. 358; C.7030; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments for suits where U.S. is interested charged to suits appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: When Army officers are defendants in suits in which the United States is interested and their defense is undertaken by the Department of Justice, their necessary expenses in attending court may be charged to the appropriation 'for defraying the expenses * * * of suits in which the United States is interested.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not entitled to mileage from Army support appropriations, such expenses are legitimate charges against the suits appropriation (51 R., 590, Mar. 2, 1887). Later practice authorized payment from contingencies for certain travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingencies cannot be used to pay compensation specifically provided elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments falling squarely into categories for which salaries or compensation are expressly provided by statute or specific appropriation may not be shifted to contingencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: payment of copyists employed in bureaus out of contingencies is prohibited by sec. 3682 R.S. because clerical compensation is specifically regulated (C.1154, Mar. 25, 1895). Also hiring beyond statutory clerk limits cannot be paid from contingencies (C.295, Sept. 15, 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation wording defines the intended scope (e.g., small-arms vs artillery)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation explicitly for 'shelter, shooting galleries, ranges, repairs, and expenses incident thereto' is intended for small-arms target practice and will not cover rental of ground for artillery practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, very small short-term rentals (a few days) might be treated as legitimate contingencies (62 P. 209, Nov. 2, 1893).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Actual necessary expenses" may substitute statutory mileage when expressly provided
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute directs that commissioners or boards shall 'serve without compensation, but shall be paid actual necessary expenses,' such expenses are chargeable to the appropriate Army appropriations and suspend ordinary mileage rules for that case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint resolution Feb. 24, 1911: commissioners to investigate maneuver grounds serve without compensation but are paid actual necessary expenses which are chargeable against Army appropriations (C.28005, Mar. 22, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Department head authorization required for contingencies under sec. 3683 R.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Under sec. 3683 R.S., expenditures from contingent funds must be authorized by the head of the department prior to incurring the expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced as a procedural constraint on use of contingencies; prior authorization is required (I Comp. Dec. 566; other cites).
